cards.title: Greedy Algorithm Fundamentals
cards.teaser: A greedy algorithm builds a solution one step at a time, always making the locally optimal choice — the best option available right now — without reconsidering earlier decisions. When the greedy-choice property holds, this produces a globally optimal solution in far less time than exhaustive search.

runs.text: Greedy

algorithms solve optimization problems by making the locally best choice at each step and never backtracking. The intuition is seductive: always pick the option that looks best right now and hope it leads to the best overall result. Sometimes it does — sometimes it doesn't.
Two structural properties must hold for a greedy algorithm to be correct:

items.text: Greedy-choice property
— a globally optimal solution can always be assembled from locally optimal choices. The greedy decision at each step is safe to commit to.
Optimal substructure
— the optimal solution to the full problem contains optimal solutions to its subproblems. (Shared with dynamic programming.)

explanation.code:
# Classic greedy example: making change with denominations [25, 10, 5, 1]
# Works ONLY because US coin denominations are carefully chosen
def make_change_greedy(amount: int) -> dict[int, int]:
    denominations = [25, 10, 5, 1]
    result: dict[int, int] = {}
    for coin in denominations:
        count, amount = divmod(amount, coin)
        if count:
            result[coin] = count
    return result

print(make_change_greedy(41))  # {25: 1, 10: 1, 5: 1, 1: 1} — 4 coins, optimal

# But with denominations [10, 6, 1], greedy FAILS for amount=12:
# Greedy picks 10 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins.  Optimal is 6 + 6 = 2 coins.
# This is why greedy correctness must be proven, not assumed.

runs.text: Greedy is not a synonym for 'fast heuristic'. It is a provably correct algorithm class when the two properties hold. When they don't, greedy produces a suboptimal or wrong answer — and you need dynamic programming or backtracking instead.

A greedy algorithm is like always eating the biggest piece of food on your plate first, without ever going back to reconsider. If eating biggest-first always results in finishing the meal optimally, it's a valid greedy strategy. If sometimes you should save a big piece to pair with a small piece, greedy fails and you need a smarter plan.

cards.title: Greedy-Choice Property and Optimal Substructure
cards.teaser: The greedy-choice property says you can safely commit to the locally best option at each step. Optimal substructure says the remaining subproblem, after a greedy choice, is also optimally solvable. Both properties together make greedy algorithms provably correct — and proving them is the real work.

runs.text: These two properties are the mathematical backbone of greedy correctness proofs. Understanding them lets you recognize when greedy is safe to use — and when it isn't.
Greedy-choice property
— for every subproblem, the greedy selection (locally optimal choice) is part of some globally optimal solution. Formally proved by an
exchange argument
: assume an optimal solution doesn't include the greedy choice; show you can swap it in without making things worse, contradicting the assumption.
Optimal substructure

— after committing to the greedy choice, the remaining problem is an instance of the same problem, and solving it optimally completes the full optimal solution. This is identical to the DP property — the difference is that greedy only needs one choice per step while DP explores all.

explanation.code:
# Proving greedy-choice property by exchange argument (pseudocode style)
# Problem: activity selection — choose max activities from non-overlapping intervals

# Greedy choice: always pick the activity that finishes earliest.
# Exchange argument proof sketch:
#   Let OPT be any optimal solution.
#   Let g = activity with earliest finish time (greedy choice).
#   If g is in OPT, we're done.
#   If g is NOT in OPT, let x be the first activity in OPT.
#   Since g finishes <= x finishes, we can replace x with g.
#   The rest of OPT is unchanged (no later conflict, since g finishes earlier).
#   The new solution is still optimal and includes g. QED.

# Optimal substructure:
#   After choosing g, the subproblem = all activities that start after g finishes.
#   This is the same problem on a smaller input — solves recursively/greedily.

runs.text: The exchange argument is the standard proof technique for greedy correctness. In interviews, being able to articulate 'I can always swap a non-greedy choice for the greedy choice without losing quality' demonstrates deep understanding. Without this, greedy is just a guess.

The greedy-choice property says: the decision that looks best right now will never need to be undone. Optimal substructure says: after making that decision, the rest of the problem is a smaller version of the same problem. Together they're a promise: commit greedily at each step and you'll reach the best possible total outcome.

cards.title: Activity Selection / Interval Scheduling
cards.teaser: Given a list of activities with start and end times, select the maximum number of non-overlapping activities. The greedy solution — always pick the activity that finishes earliest — runs in O(n log n) and is provably optimal via the exchange argument.

runs.text: Interval scheduling maximization
is the canonical greedy problem. You have a single resource (a meeting room, a CPU) and a set of intervals. You want to fit as many intervals as possible without overlap.
The greedy strategy is: sort activities by
finish time

, then repeatedly select the next activity whose start time is at or after the last chosen activity's finish time. This is the correct greedy choice — earlier finish time leaves the most room for future activities.

explanation.code:
def activity_selection(
    activities: list[tuple[int, int]]   # (start, finish)
) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    # Sort by finish time — the greedy-choice ordering
    sorted_acts = sorted(activities, key=lambda x: x[1])
    selected: list[tuple[int, int]] = []
    last_finish = -1

    for start, finish in sorted_acts:
        if start >= last_finish:   # no overlap with last selected
            selected.append((start, finish))
            last_finish = finish

    return selected

# Example: 6 activities
activities = [(1, 4), (3, 5), (0, 6), (5, 7), (3, 9), (5, 9), (6, 10), (8, 11)]
print(activity_selection(activities))
# [(1, 4), (5, 7), (8, 11)] — 3 activities, maximum possible

# Time: O(n log n) for sort + O(n) scan = O(n log n)
# Space: O(n) for the result

# Variant: interval scheduling minimization (minimize number of rooms)
# = find maximum number of overlapping intervals at any point
# Use a sweep-line with a min-heap of finish times

runs.text: The key insight: finishing earliest is always at least as good as any other choice. It doesn't restrict future choices more than necessary. Sorting by start time or shortest duration does NOT work — try [(1,10), (2,3), (9,11)] sorted by start: greedy picks (1,10) and misses the optimal (2,3)+(9,11).

You have one meeting room and a pile of meeting requests with start/end times. To fit the most meetings, always book whichever unscheduled meeting ends the soonest. That's it. Ending early leaves the room available sooner, maximizing future options. Sort by finish time, scan once, pick every meeting that fits — done in near-linear time.

cards.title: Huffman Coding
cards.teaser: Huffman coding assigns variable-length bit strings to symbols, giving shorter codes to more frequent symbols. Built bottom-up using a min-heap, it produces the optimal prefix-free code — the theoretical minimum average bits per symbol — in O(n log n).

runs.text: Huffman coding
is the foundation of lossless compression (ZIP, PNG, JPEG entropy stage, HTTP/2 headers). Each symbol gets a unique binary code such that no code is a prefix of another (
prefix-free
), enabling unambiguous decoding. Frequent symbols get short codes; rare ones get long codes.

The greedy algorithm: repeatedly merge the two lowest-frequency nodes into a new parent node whose frequency is their sum. A min-heap makes extracting the two smallest O(log n). The resulting binary tree defines the codes: left edge = 0, right edge = 1, code for each symbol = path from root to leaf.

explanation.code:
import heapq
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any

@dataclass(order=True)
class HuffNode:
    freq: int
    symbol: str | None = field(compare=False, default=None)
    left: Any = field(compare=False, default=None)
    right: Any = field(compare=False, default=None)

def build_huffman_tree(freqs: dict[str, int]) -> HuffNode:
    heap = [HuffNode(f, s) for s, f in freqs.items()]
    heapq.heapify(heap)

    while len(heap) > 1:
        left = heapq.heappop(heap)   # smallest freq
        right = heapq.heappop(heap)  # second smallest
        merged = HuffNode(left.freq + right.freq, left=left, right=right)
        heapq.heappush(heap, merged)

    return heap[0]   # root of Huffman tree

def build_codes(node: HuffNode, prefix: str = '') -> dict[str, str]:
    if node.symbol is not None:          # leaf node
        return {node.symbol: prefix or '0'}  # single-symbol edge case
    codes: dict[str, str] = {}
    if node.left:  codes.update(build_codes(node.left,  prefix + '0'))
    if node.right: codes.update(build_codes(node.right, prefix + '1'))
    return codes

# Example: English-like frequencies
freqs = {'e': 120, 't': 90, 'a': 80, 'i': 70, 'n': 60, 'z': 3}
tree = build_huffman_tree(freqs)
codes = build_codes(tree)
for sym in sorted(freqs, key=freqs.get, reverse=True):  # type: ignore
    print(f"'{sym}' (freq={freqs[sym]}): {codes[sym]}")
# 'e' (freq=120): 11    (2 bits — most frequent)
# 'z' (freq=3):   0000  (4 bits — least frequent)

runs.text: Huffman coding achieves the Shannon entropy lower bound — no other prefix-free code can have a smaller average code length given the same symbol frequencies. The greedy choice (merge two smallest) is proved optimal: merging smallest-frequency nodes last would push them deepest in the tree, maximizing their already-high contribution to average length.

Imagine encoding a book where 'e' appears 10,000 times and 'z' appears 5 times. With fixed-width codes, both get 8 bits. Huffman says: give 'e' a 2-bit code and 'z' a 10-bit code — the total bits saved on 'e' vastly outweigh the bits added to 'z'. Build a tree by repeatedly merging the two cheapest symbols, and the tree tells you each symbol's optimal code.

cards.title: Fractional Knapsack vs 0/1 Knapsack
cards.teaser: Fractional knapsack — where you can take fractions of items — is solved optimally by greedy: sort by value/weight ratio and take greedily. The 0/1 variant (take all or nothing) breaks the greedy-choice property and requires dynamic programming in O(nW).

runs.text: The knapsack problem is a perfect case study in when greedy works and when it doesn't, because the two variants look nearly identical but require fundamentally different algorithms.

items.text: Fractional knapsack
— you can take any fraction of an item. Greedy is optimal: sort by value-per-unit-weight, take items greedily until the knapsack is full, then take a fraction of the next item.
0/1 knapsack
— each item is taken in full or not at all. Greedy fails because taking the highest ratio item may prevent fitting two lower-ratio items that together have higher total value.

explanation.code:
# Fractional Knapsack — greedy works
def fractional_knapsack(
    items: list[tuple[float, float]],   # (value, weight)
    capacity: float
) -> float:
    # Sort by value-per-weight ratio, descending
    ratio_items = sorted(items, key=lambda x: x[0] / x[1], reverse=True)
    total_value = 0.0
    remaining = capacity

    for value, weight in ratio_items:
        if remaining <= 0:
            break
        take = min(weight, remaining)      # take fraction if needed
        total_value += value * (take / weight)
        remaining -= take

    return total_value

items = [(60, 10), (100, 20), (120, 30)]   # (value, weight)
print(fractional_knapsack(items, capacity=50))  # 240.0 — optimal

# 0/1 Knapsack — greedy FAILS, need DP
# Items: (60,10), (100,20), (120,30) — capacity 50
# Greedy by ratio: takes all of item1 (6.0/unit) + item2 (5.0/unit) = 160 value, 30 weight used; then item3 20/30 fraction = 80 — but 0/1 means no fractions!
# Greedy picks items 1+2 = 160. But items 2+3 = 220 (fits in 50). Greedy is wrong.
def knapsack_01(items: list[tuple[int, int]], W: int) -> int:
    n = len(items)
    dp = [[0] * (W + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i, (v, w) in enumerate(items, 1):
        for cap in range(W + 1):
            dp[i][cap] = dp[i-1][cap]
            if w <= cap:
                dp[i][cap] = max(dp[i][cap], dp[i-1][cap-w] + v)
    return dp[n][W]

print(knapsack_01([(60,10),(100,20),(120,30)], 50))  # 220

runs.text: The difference: in fractional knapsack, you can always 'use up' the remaining capacity with a piece of the next item, so the greedy-choice property holds. In 0/1 knapsack, you can't split items, so committing to a high-ratio item may block a better combination — breaking the greedy-choice property.

Fractional knapsack is like filling a bag with gold dust — take the densest gold first, and if the bag isn't full, pour in some silver dust. Greedy works because you can always use leftover space. 0/1 knapsack is like choosing whole gold bars — you can't cut them. Sometimes skipping a high-density bar lets you fit two medium bars worth more in total. That subtlety kills greedy and demands DP.

cards.title: Greedy vs DP: When Greedy Fails
cards.teaser: Greedy fails when a locally optimal choice forecloses better global options. Coin change with arbitrary denominations is the textbook example: greedy may miss the optimal number of coins, while DP explores all combinations and guarantees the minimum. The failure condition is always a broken greedy-choice property.

runs.text: The decision between greedy and DP reduces to one question:
does the locally optimal choice remain valid globally?
Greedy requires this. DP does not — it evaluates all possible decisions at each step and picks the one with the best downstream result.

explanation.code:
# Coin change: minimum coins to make 'amount'
# With denominations [1, 5, 10, 25] — greedy works (canonical system)
# With denominations [1, 3, 4] — greedy FAILS for amount=6
#   Greedy: 4+1+1 = 3 coins.  Optimal: 3+3 = 2 coins.

# Greedy (only correct for canonical coin systems)
def coin_change_greedy(coins: list[int], amount: int) -> int:
    coins.sort(reverse=True)
    count = 0
    for coin in coins:
        count += amount // coin
        amount %= coin
    return count if amount == 0 else -1

# DP (always correct)
def coin_change_dp(coins: list[int], amount: int) -> int:
    dp = [float('inf')] * (amount + 1)
    dp[0] = 0
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        for coin in coins:
            if coin <= a and dp[a - coin] + 1 < dp[a]:
                dp[a] = dp[a - coin] + 1
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != float('inf') else -1

# [1, 3, 4], amount=6
print(coin_change_greedy([1, 3, 4], 6))  # 3 (wrong: 4+1+1)
print(coin_change_dp([1, 3, 4], 6))      # 2 (correct: 3+3)

# When does greedy work for coin change?
# If every denomination divides cleanly into the next (1, 5, 25, 125...)
# or the system is 'canonical' — provable but complex to verify in general.

items.text: Use greedy
when you can prove the greedy-choice property — typically via exchange argument.
Use DP
when subproblems overlap and the greedy choice might exclude a better global solution.
Use backtracking
when constraints are complex and the solution space must be explored explicitly.

runs.text: Dijkstra's algorithm is itself a greedy algorithm — and it works because non-negative edge weights guarantee that finalized shortest distances will never be improved later. If negative edges existed (breaking this guarantee), greedy would fail and you'd need Bellman-Ford.

Greedy and DP are both about making choices step by step. Greedy commits: once you pick, you never look back. DP explores: at each step it considers every option and picks what's best given all future consequences. Greedy is faster but only correct when the first-choice is always safe. DP is slower but always finds the global optimum. Coin change with weird denominations shows exactly where greedy's commit-and-forget strategy breaks down.

cards.title: Backtracking Pattern
cards.teaser: Backtracking is a systematic search strategy: build the solution incrementally, abandon (prune) a partial solution as soon as it violates constraints, and backtrack to the last valid state to try a different option. It solves N-Queens, Sudoku, permutations, and combinatorial puzzles — typically exponential in worst case, but pruning makes it practical.

runs.text: Backtracking
is depth-first search over a decision tree. At each node you make a choice, recurse, and — if the choice leads to a dead end — undo it (
backtrack
) and try another. The critical optimization is
pruning
: detecting dead ends early, before recursing into the full subtree.

explanation.code:
# N-Queens: place N queens on an N×N board so none attack each other
def solve_n_queens(n: int) -> list[list[int]]:
    results: list[list[int]] = []
    # queens[row] = column index of queen in that row
    queens: list[int] = []

    def is_valid(row: int, col: int) -> bool:
        for r, c in enumerate(queens):
            if c == col:                    # same column
                return False
            if abs(r - row) == abs(c - col):  # same diagonal
                return False
        return True

    def backtrack(row: int) -> None:
        if row == n:
            results.append(queens.copy())  # found a solution
            return
        for col in range(n):
            if is_valid(row, col):          # prune invalid placements
                queens.append(col)          # make choice
                backtrack(row + 1)          # recurse
                queens.pop()               # undo choice (backtrack)

    backtrack(0)
    return results

solutions = solve_n_queens(4)
print(f"{len(solutions)} solutions for 4-queens")
for s in solutions:
    print(s)   # [1, 3, 0, 2] and [2, 0, 3, 1]

# General backtracking template:
# def backtrack(state):
#     if is_solution(state): record(state); return
#     for choice in get_choices(state):
#         if is_valid(state, choice):
#             apply(state, choice)      # make choice
#             backtrack(new_state)      # explore
#             undo(state, choice)       # backtrack

runs.text: Backtracking is the right tool when: the solution is a sequence of choices, constraints can be checked incrementally, and the solution space is too large for brute force but pruning eliminates large subtrees. Classic problems: N-Queens, Sudoku solver, word search on a grid, generating all permutations/subsets/combinations, crossword filling.

Backtracking is solving a maze by always going forward until you hit a wall, then stepping back to the last fork and trying a different turn. You never randomly jump around — you systematically explore every path while cutting off dead ends as soon as you see them. The 'undo' step is what makes it backtracking instead of plain DFS: you restore state so you can try the next option cleanly.

cards.title: Branch and Bound
cards.teaser: Branch and bound is backtracking with an optimistic upper (or lower) bound computed at each node. If the best possible value achievable from the current node is worse than the best solution already found, prune the entire subtree. It finds exact optimal solutions to NP-hard problems faster than brute-force.

runs.text: Branch and bound
extends backtracking by adding a
bounding function

— a fast estimate of the best possible outcome reachable from the current partial solution. If this bound is worse than the best complete solution found so far, the subtree is pruned entirely. This turns exponential search into something tractable for moderate-sized inputs.

items.text: Branch
— divide the problem into subproblems (yes/no for including each item in 0/1 knapsack; left/right subtree in TSP).
Bound
— compute an optimistic bound for each subproblem (e.g., fractional knapsack relaxation gives an upper bound for 0/1 knapsack value).
Prune
— if bound ≤ best known solution, discard the subproblem — no solution in this subtree can improve the answer.

explanation.code:
import heapq
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

# Branch and Bound for 0/1 Knapsack (maximization)
# Bound: fractional knapsack relaxation on remaining items
@dataclass(order=True)
class Node:
    neg_bound: float    # negated for min-heap (we maximize)
    level: int = field(compare=False)
    value: float = field(compare=False)
    weight: float = field(compare=False)

def bnb_knapsack(
    items: list[tuple[float, float]],  # (value, weight)
    capacity: float
) -> float:
    # Sort items by value/weight ratio (greedy order for bounding)
    items = sorted(items, key=lambda x: x[0]/x[1], reverse=True)
    n = len(items)

    def upper_bound(level: int, value: float, weight: float) -> float:
        """Fractional knapsack bound from 'level' onward."""
        bound = value
        remaining = capacity - weight
        for i in range(level, n):
            v, w = items[i]
            if w <= remaining:
                bound += v; remaining -= w
            else:
                bound += v * (remaining / w); break
        return bound

    best = 0.0
    heap: list[Node] = [Node(-upper_bound(0, 0, 0), 0, 0, 0)]

    while heap:
        node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if node.level == n: continue
        v, w = items[node.level]
        # Branch: include item
        new_w = node.weight + w
        new_v = node.value + v
        if new_w <= capacity:
            best = max(best, new_v)
            ub = upper_bound(node.level + 1, new_v, new_w)
            if ub > best:
                heapq.heappush(heap, Node(-ub, node.level+1, new_v, new_w))
        # Branch: exclude item
        ub = upper_bound(node.level + 1, node.value, node.weight)
        if ub > best:
            heapq.heappush(heap, Node(-ub, node.level+1, node.value, node.weight))

    return best

runs.text: Branch and bound is used in real solvers: linear programming branch-and-bound for integer programming (MIP solvers like Gurobi, CPLEX), TSP solvers, and constraint programming. The quality of the bounding function is everything — a tight bound prunes aggressively; a loose bound is barely better than brute force.

Branch and bound is backtracking with a crystal ball. At each fork in the decision tree, you ask: 'Even in the best case, what's the most I could gain by going down this path?' If the answer is less than what you've already found, don't bother going down. The crystal ball doesn't need to be exact — just optimistic enough to safely prune. The better your estimate, the more you prune, the faster it runs.

cards.title: Divide and Conquer (Advanced View)
cards.teaser: Divide and conquer splits a problem into independent subproblems, solves each recursively, and combines the results. The Master Theorem gives the time complexity for T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) in closed form. Advanced applications include Karatsuba multiplication (O(n^1.585)) and merge sort's inversion count.

runs.text: Divide and conquer has three phases:
divide
(split into b subproblems of size n/b),
conquer
(solve each recursively), and
combine
(merge results). Unlike DP, subproblems are independent — no overlapping work to memoize. The recurrence T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) describes the runtime, solved by the Master Theorem.

explanation.code:
# Master Theorem: T(n) = aT(n/b) + O(n^d)
# Compute c = log_b(a)  (critical exponent)
# Case 1: d < c  → T(n) = O(n^c)           [recursion dominates]
# Case 2: d = c  → T(n) = O(n^c * log n)   [tied — log factor]
# Case 3: d > c  → T(n) = O(n^d)           [combine dominates]

# Examples:
# Merge sort:  a=2, b=2, d=1 → c=1 → Case 2: O(n log n)
# Binary search: a=1, b=2, d=0 → c=0 → Case 2: O(log n)
# Karatsuba:   a=3, b=2, d=1 → c=log2(3)≈1.585 > 1 → Case 1: O(n^1.585)

# Counting inversions (# pairs i<j where arr[i]>arr[j]) via modified merge sort
def count_inversions(arr: list[int]) -> tuple[list[int], int]:
    if len(arr) <= 1:
        return arr, 0
    mid = len(arr) // 2
    left, left_inv = count_inversions(arr[:mid])
    right, right_inv = count_inversions(arr[mid:])
    merged: list[int] = []
    inversions = left_inv + right_inv
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            merged.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            # All remaining left elements form inversions with right[j]
            inversions += len(left) - i
            merged.append(right[j]); j += 1
    merged.extend(left[i:])
    merged.extend(right[j:])
    return merged, inversions

_, inv = count_inversions([3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6])
print(f"Inversions: {inv}")  # 7

runs.text: Divide and conquer differs from DP in one key way: subproblems do not overlap. Merge sort splits into left and right halves — they share no elements. Fibonacci's recursion splits into overlapping subproblems (fib(4) calls fib(3) and fib(2); fib(3) also calls fib(2)) — that's DP territory. No overlap = D&C. Overlap = DP.

Divide and conquer is like sorting a deck of cards by splitting it in half, having two friends sort their halves independently, then merging the two sorted halves. The two friends work independently — no coordination needed mid-sort. The Master Theorem is just a formula for predicting how long this kind of recursive splitting takes, based on how many pieces you split into, how big each piece is, and how expensive the merge step is.

cards.title: Bit Manipulation Tricks
cards.teaser: Bit manipulation solves common problems in O(1) using bitwise operators: XOR finds the lone non-duplicate, n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit (counts set bits in O(popcount)), and n & -n isolates the lowest set bit. These tricks appear constantly in low-level code, competitive programming, and hardware interfaces.

runs.text: Bitwise operators work directly on the binary representation of integers. Six operators: AND
, OR
, XOR
, NOT
, left-shift
, right-shift
. The most useful tricks come from XOR and the
identity.

explanation.code:
# --- Core tricks ---

# 1. XOR: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x → finds the single non-duplicate
def find_single(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    result = 0
    for n in nums: result ^= n
    return result
print(find_single([2, 3, 2, 4, 3]))  # 4  (O(n) time, O(1) space)

# 2. n & (n-1): clears lowest set bit → count set bits (Brian Kernighan's)
def count_set_bits(n: int) -> int:
    count = 0
    while n:
        n &= n - 1  # clears the rightmost 1-bit
        count += 1
    return count
print(count_set_bits(0b101101))  # 4

# 3. n & -n: isolates lowest set bit
def lowest_set_bit(n: int) -> int:
    return n & -n
print(bin(lowest_set_bit(0b101100)))  # 0b100 (bit 2)

# 4. Power of two check: power of 2 has exactly one set bit
def is_power_of_two(n: int) -> bool:
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0
print(is_power_of_two(64))   # True
print(is_power_of_two(60))   # False

# 5. Swap without temp variable (XOR swap)
def xor_swap(a: int, b: int) -> tuple[int, int]:
    a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b
    return a, b

# 6. Check if k-th bit is set (0-indexed from right)
def is_kth_bit_set(n: int, k: int) -> bool:
    return bool(n & (1 << k))

# 7. Set / clear / toggle k-th bit
set_bit   = lambda n, k: n |  (1 << k)
clear_bit = lambda n, k: n & ~(1 << k)
toggle_bit = lambda n, k: n ^ (1 << k)

runs.text: Python's integers are arbitrary precision — no overflow. But int.bit_count() (Python 3.10+) gives popcount directly. In C/C++/Java, use __builtin_popcount() or Integer.bitCount() for hardware-accelerated popcount. XOR is especially powerful for parity and cryptography: XOR is its own inverse, so a ^ b ^ b == a.

Bit tricks exploit the binary representation of numbers. XOR is magic: anything XORed with itself is zero, and anything XORed with zero is itself — so XOR-ing an array where every number appears twice except one leaves only the singleton. The n & (n-1) trick works because subtracting 1 flips all bits from the lowest 1-bit rightward, and ANDing with n zeroes exactly those bits — clearing one 1-bit per iteration.

cards.title: String Algorithms: KMP and Rabin-Karp
cards.teaser: KMP finds all occurrences of a pattern P in text T in O(n + m) by precomputing a failure function that avoids re-scanning matched characters. Rabin-Karp uses a rolling hash for expected O(n + m) search and excels at multi-pattern search. Both beat the naive O(nm) approach.

runs.text: Naive substring search compares the pattern at every position, giving O(nm) in the worst case. For n = 10^6 and m = 10^3, that's 10^9 operations. KMP and Rabin-Karp both reduce this to O(n + m).

explanation.code:
# KMP — Knuth-Morris-Pratt
def kmp_search(text: str, pattern: str) -> list[int]:
    def build_failure(p: str) -> list[int]:
        """failure[i] = length of longest proper prefix of p[:i+1] that is also a suffix."""
        f = [0] * len(p)
        k = 0
        for i in range(1, len(p)):
            while k > 0 and p[i] != p[k]:
                k = f[k - 1]   # fall back using failure function
            if p[i] == p[k]:
                k += 1
            f[i] = k
        return f

    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)
    if m == 0: return []
    failure = build_failure(pattern)
    matches: list[int] = []
    k = 0   # matched characters so far
    for i in range(n):
        while k > 0 and text[i] != pattern[k]:
            k = failure[k - 1]   # don't re-scan; fall back
        if text[i] == pattern[k]:
            k += 1
        if k == m:
            matches.append(i - m + 1)   # full match ending at i
            k = failure[k - 1]           # look for overlapping matches
    return matches

print(kmp_search('ababcabcababd', 'ababd'))  # [7]

# Rabin-Karp — rolling hash
def rabin_karp(text: str, pattern: str, base: int = 256, mod: int = 10**9+7) -> list[int]:
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)
    if m > n: return []
    h = pow(base, m - 1, mod)      # base^(m-1) mod prime
    p_hash = t_hash = 0
    for i in range(m):
        p_hash = (p_hash * base + ord(pattern[i])) % mod
        t_hash = (t_hash * base + ord(text[i])) % mod
    matches: list[int] = []
    for i in range(n - m + 1):
        if t_hash == p_hash and text[i:i+m] == pattern:  # hash match + verify
            matches.append(i)
        if i < n - m:
            t_hash = (base * (t_hash - ord(text[i]) * h) + ord(text[i + m])) % mod
    return matches

print(rabin_karp('ababcababd', 'abab'))  # [0, 5]

runs.text: KMP is deterministically O(n + m) — the failure function guarantees no character in the text is compared more than twice. Rabin-Karp is O(n + m) expected, O(nm) worst case (if every hash matches but the strings differ — a 'spurious hit'). Rabin-Karp shines for multi-pattern search: hash all k patterns once, then a single pass finds any match in O(n + km) vs O(nkm) naively.

KMP is smart substring search. Instead of restarting from scratch after a mismatch, it uses a precomputed table that says 'you matched this much — here's the longest prefix of the pattern that could still be a suffix of what you've matched so far, so resume from there.' This prevents ever stepping backward in the text. Rabin-Karp takes a different approach: hash the pattern, then slide a window over the text maintaining a rolling hash — only do a full character comparison when hashes match.

cards.title: Approximation Algorithms and NP-Hard Problems
cards.teaser: NP-hard problems (TSP, Set Cover, vertex cover) have no known polynomial-time exact algorithms. Approximation algorithms sacrifice exactness for speed: a 2-approximation for vertex cover, an O(log n)-approximation for Set Cover, and a 1.5-approximation (Christofides) for metric TSP — all with provable worst-case bounds.

runs.text: NP-hard

problems are at least as hard as the hardest problems in NP. No polynomial-time algorithm is known for any of them (and the P ≠ NP conjecture says none exists). For large inputs, exact algorithms become infeasible.
Approximation algorithms
return provably near-optimal solutions in polynomial time — guaranteed to be within a factor α of optimal.

items.text: Vertex Cover (2-approximation)
— repeatedly pick any uncovered edge, add both endpoints to the cover, remove all edges they cover. Result is at most 2× optimal.
Set Cover (O(log n)-approximation)
— greedy: always pick the set covering the most uncovered elements. Achieves O(log n) approximation ratio — provably tight.
Metric TSP (2-approximation via MST)
— build an MST, do a DFS traversal to get a Hamiltonian path, shortcut repeated vertices. Christofides improves to 1.5× using minimum-weight perfect matching.

explanation.code:
# Greedy Set Cover — O(log n) approximation
def set_cover(
    universe: set[int], sets: list[set[int]]
) -> list[int]:
    uncovered = set(universe)
    chosen: list[int] = []
    used = [False] * len(sets)

    while uncovered:
        # Greedy: pick the set covering the most uncovered elements
        best_idx = max(
            (i for i in range(len(sets)) if not used[i]),
            key=lambda i: len(sets[i] & uncovered)
        )
        chosen.append(best_idx)
        uncovered -= sets[best_idx]
        used[best_idx] = True

    return chosen

universe = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}
sets = [{1,2,3,4}, {2,4,6}, {3,5,7}, {1,5,6,7}]
chosen = set_cover(universe, sets)
print([list(sets[i]) for i in chosen])
# [[1,2,3,4], [3,5,7]] — covers all 7 elements with 2 sets

# MST-based 2-approximation for metric TSP
import itertools, heapq

def tsp_mst_approx(dist: list[list[float]]) -> tuple[list[int], float]:
    n = len(dist)
    # Prim's MST
    in_mst = [False] * n
    key = [float('inf')] * n; key[0] = 0
    parent = [-1] * n
    heap = [(0.0, 0)]
    while heap:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if in_mst[u]: continue
        in_mst[u] = True
        for v in range(n):
            if not in_mst[v] and dist[u][v] < key[v]:
                key[v] = dist[u][v]; parent[v] = u
                heapq.heappush(heap, (key[v], v))
    # DFS pre-order on MST → tour (shortcutting repeated vertices)
    adj: list[list[int]] = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for v in range(1, n): adj[parent[v]].append(v)
    visited = [False] * n
    tour: list[int] = []
    stack = [0]
    while stack:
        u = stack.pop()
        if visited[u]: continue
        visited[u] = True; tour.append(u)
        for v in reversed(adj[u]): stack.append(v)
    total = sum(dist[tour[i]][tour[i+1]] for i in range(n-1)) + dist[tour[-1]][tour[0]]
    return tour, total

runs.text: NP-hard doesn't mean impossible — it means 'no polynomial-time exact algorithm is known'. In practice: for small inputs use exact methods (branch and bound); for large inputs use approximation algorithms with guaranteed bounds; for practical heuristics use local search (2-opt for TSP), simulated annealing, or genetic algorithms — these have no worst-case guarantee but work well empirically.

NP-hard problems are the class of problems where every known algorithm either runs in exponential time or gives approximate answers. A 2-approximation algorithm is a guarantee: 'I can't find the exact optimum quickly, but I promise my answer is at most twice as bad as optimal.' For the TSP, build the cheapest spanning tree, take a walk through it, and shortcut any revisited cities — this is always within 2× the optimal tour length. Not perfect, but provably bounded and fast.
